title: How to Get Rich
summary: Long interview series on the 'How to Get Rich' tweetstorm: wealth comes from equity, specific knowledge, accountability and leverage compounded over decades; get-rich-quick schemes are someone else getting rich off you.

assertions.quote: You are not going to get rich renting out your time. You must own equity, a piece of the business to gain your financial freedom.

verdicts.note: Wealth surveys show most large fortunes come from business ownership and assets, but high-earning salaried professionals do accumulate wealth by saving and investing.

assertions.quote: There are no get rich quick schemes. That’s just someone else getting rich off you.

verdicts.note: FTC business-opportunity cases and MLM income disclosures consistently show the seller profits while most buyers lose money, though rare individual windfalls exist.

Nudge took over $400 million in revenue from 2014-2017 selling house-flipping training while more than 95% of attendees paid more than they netted; one scheme illustrating the seller profiting at buyers' expense.

assertions.quote: Avoid people who got rich quickly. They’re just giving you their winning lottery ticket numbers.

verdicts.note: Survivorship bias is well documented; the specific path of a rapid success rarely replicates because luck and timing dominated it.

assertions.quote: you don’t want to learn how to be rich from somebody who makes their money by telling people how to be rich. It’s suspect.

verdicts.note: A credibility heuristic rather than a measurable claim, though it matches enforcement cases where coaching revenue dwarfed the taught method's own returns.
Nudge's $400 million came from selling real-estate training, and over 95% of its seminar attendees lost money net; consistent with the heuristic for this scheme.

assertions.quote: My personal wealth has not been generated by one big year. It stacks up little bit, chips at a time.

verdicts.note: Most self-made millionaires reach it in their 40s and 50s after decades of accumulation, though tech exits give a minority lumpy, lottery-like outcomes.

assertions.quote: This newest form of leverage is where all the new fortunes are made, all the new billionaires.

verdicts.note: Zero-marginal-cost products do underlie many recent fortunes, but creator and software income is power-law distributed and most participants earn little.
Zero-marginal-cost products underlie many recent fortunes, but building them takes labor and often capital, and outcomes are power-law with most participants earning little.

assertions.quote: A lot of people think making money is about luck. It’s not. It’s about becoming the kind of person that makes money.

verdicts.note: Previously successful founders do have higher success rates on their next venture, but studies of entrepreneurial outcomes still show a large luck component.

In the model skill raises the odds but is far from sufficient: medium-high talent is often necessary, yet the most talented agents (T > 0.8) are the top performer in only 3% of runs and only about a third of highly talented agents end above their starting capital, contradicting the skill-not-luck framing; rebuilding wealth in a decade is not modelled.
Skill raises the odds, but research on entrepreneurial and wealth outcomes finds a large luck component, so neither 'not luck' nor a reliable decade-long rebuild holds.

assertions.quote: your returns just devolve into your cost of training plus the return on investment on that training.

verdicts.note: Scarce, hard-to-codify skills do earn a premium, but many trainable credentialed professions still pay very well because entry is restricted.

assertions.quote: Nobody really works 80 to 120 hours a week at high output, with mental clarity. Your brain breaks down.

verdicts.note: Pencavel's munitions-worker data and later studies show output per hour falls steeply beyond about 50 hours a week.

assertions.quote: but when they win they win big. On average they’ll make more.

verdicts.note: Mean self-employment income is pulled up by a few large exits, but median self-employed earnings are at or below comparable wage employment.

Incorporated entrepreneurs have much fatter-tailed earnings than salaried workers (the 90th-percentile incorporated earns 70% more than the 90th-percentile salaried worker) and average 48% higher residual hourly earnings, but the aggregate median self-employed earns about 15% less and the median unincorporated owner about 30% less than comparable employees, and the authors do not assess risk-adjusted returns or losses; 'earn more on average' holds for incorporated entrepreneurs, not business owners generally.

assertions.quote: Don’t bet everything on one big gamble. Be careful how much you bet each time, so you don’t lose the whole kitty.

verdicts.note: Kelly-criterion and ergodicity arguments show that full-stake bets with positive expectation still go bust with probability approaching one over repeated play.

assertions.quote: Everybody can be wealthy. Everybody can be retired. Everybody can be successful. It is merely a question of education and desire.

verdicts.note: Aggregate wealth has grown enormously, but relative wealth and the scarce resources that define being rich are constrained, so universal wealth does not follow.
Total wealth grows, but being wealthy is largely relative and scarce assets are constrained, so positive-sum growth does not mean everyone can become wealthy.
